lead: Agile development builds software in short repeated increments, with the customer close to the team and able to change the plan between increments. It exists because waterfall projects deliver late and handle change badly. Agile is used in product companies, client projects, and banks or government systems where requirements move. Extreme Programming (XP) is one agile process that adds engineering practices such as test-first coding, pair programming and refactoring, so fast change does not lower quality.
prereq: You need 1.4 for the generic process framework and 1.5 for waterfall and incremental delivery; agile is an incremental model with specific values.

blocks.text: Waterfall asks the customer to approve all requirements before coding. The customer sees the system at the end. If a rule changes in month eight, the team learns after design is signed off. Agile answers with a small working part every few weeks and a customer who says whether it is right.
The Agile Manifesto (2001) states four values. The right-hand items still matter; the left-hand items matter more.

items: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.
Responding to change over following a plan.

blocks.text: Principles follow: deliver in short increments, welcome changing requirements, business people and developers talk daily, working software is the main measure of progress, keep design simple, and self-organising teams decide how work is done.
A story point is a relative size estimate for one feature, agreed by the team, not a unit of time. Velocity is a planning number, not a progress measure.
velocity = story points finished ÷ number of iterations
blocks.where: velocity is average story points completed per iteration; for one fixed-length iteration it is just the points finished in that sprint.

blocks.text: Use velocity for the next two or three iterations only. It is not a target to raise by pressure.
Scrum is the most widely used agile framework. It keeps one list of work and runs fixed-length sprints, usually 2 to 4 weeks.

Three roles. The product owner owns the backlog and decides priority and value. The Scrum master removes blockers and guards the process; this is not the team's manager. The team, usually five to nine people, does design, coding and testing.

Three artifacts. The product backlog is the ordered list of everything wanted, written as user stories. The sprint backlog is the subset committed for the current sprint. The increment is working, tested software from the sprint.

Four events. Sprint planning selects backlog items and a sprint goal. The daily scrum is a 15-minute stand-up: done, next, blockers. The sprint review shows the increment to stakeholders. The retrospective picks one improvement.
Two rules protect the rhythm. Sprint length stays fixed. Once a sprint starts, only the product owner may change its goal, and only if the sprint has become pointless.
XP has twelve practices, best learned in groups.

items: Planning: planning game (customer writes stories, team estimates, together they pick the next release), small releases, on-site customer.
Design: simple design, metaphor (one shared story of the system), refactoring.
Coding: test-first development, pair programming, coding standards, collective ownership.
Integration: continuous integration (merge and build many times a day).
Sustainable pace: a 40-hour week, because tired developers write defects.

blocks.text: Test-first development, now test-driven development (TDD), runs a short cycle. Write a test for the next small behaviour and watch it fail (red). Write the least code that passes (green). Refactor with the test as a safety net. Tests pile up into a regression suite, which makes refactoring and continuous integration safe.

In pair programming two developers share one machine. One drives (types), one navigates (thinks ahead, questions design), and they swap. It is continuous code review. Pairing costs some raw speed and repays it in fewer defects and faster knowledge spread. Collective ownership and rotation stop code depending on one person.

head: Aspect
Conventional (plan-driven)
Agile
rows: Fixed early, change by change control
As needed, for team and users

blocks.text: Neither is always right. Plan-driven work suits fixed contracts and safety-critical systems with audited specifications. Agile suits products where markets or rules move. A practical project may mix: a short up-front study of the highest-risk requirements, then agile increments. Agile is not a licence to skip planning or documentation; it plans every iteration and documents what users, auditors or new team members actually need.

figure.caption: Each bar is one 2-week sprint at the pairing-reduced velocity of 8 points: three sprints reach 24 of the 31 backlog points, so the fourth sprint delivers the last 7 and the work ends at week 8.

spec.aria: A four-sprint timeline over eight weeks: each of the first three 2-week sprints delivers 8 story points, reaching 24 of 31, and the fourth sprint delivers the last 7 points.

examples.question: A team runs 2-week sprints with velocity 10 story points per sprint. Backlog: login 5, search 8, report 3, payment 13, help 2. The team adopts XP pair programming, and the coach estimates a 20% drop in capacity. How many 2-week sprints are needed for the whole backlog, and how many weeks?
steps: Check: 3 sprints give 24 points, leaving 7; 4 sprints give 32 points.

Ranking comes from the product owner, not the estimates. Suppose the product owner ranks payment and login highest, then search, report, help. The team builds in that order, splitting any story too large for one sprint, so if it stops after 3 sprints the most valuable features are already delivered; size and value are different.
examples.answer: The backlog is 31 story points; at velocity 8 the team needs 4 sprints, that is 8 weeks, and must not promise delivery in 3 sprints.
examples.check:
import math
total = 5 + 8 + 3 + 13 + 2
vel = 10 * (1 - 0.20)
sprints = math.ceil(total / vel)
weeks = sprints * 2
print(total)
print(vel)
print(sprints)
print(weeks)

examples.question: A team has velocity 12 points per 2-week sprint. It adopts TDD and pair programming, cutting capacity by 25%. The backlog totals 60 points. How many sprints are needed?
steps: Check: 6 sprints give 54 points, short by 6; 7 sprints give 63 points.
examples.answer: 7 sprints of 2 weeks, that is 14 weeks.
examples.check:
import math
vel = 12 * 0.75
print(vel)
print(math.ceil(60 / vel))

traps: Saying agile means no plan and no documentation. Agile plans every sprint and writes documents users, auditors or new members need.
Confusing the product backlog with the sprint backlog. The product backlog is everything wanted; the sprint backlog is the fixed subset for the current sprint.
Thinking velocity can be raised by pressure. It is a measured average for short-term planning; treating it as a target corrupts estimates.
Believing pair programming means two people type the same line. One drives, one navigates, and they swap.
Calling the Scrum master the team's manager. That role removes blockers; the product owner owns priority and value.

quiz.q: State the four values of the Agile Manifesto.
quiz.a: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan.

quiz.q: Why does agile development welcome changing requirements instead of freezing them early?
quiz.a: Only a working increment shows what the customer needs, and short iterations are cheap to redirect. Requirements stay in a prioritised backlog, so change is absorbed at the next iteration boundary.

quiz.q: A team has velocity 12 story points per 2-week sprint and a backlog of 30 points. How many sprints are needed?
quiz.a: ceil(30 ÷ 12) = 3 sprints. Two sprints give 24 points, leaving 6, so a third is needed. Total time = 6 weeks.

quiz.q: A manager says: we are agile now, so the team will stop writing design documents and test plans. Analyse what is wrong.
quiz.a: Agile changes when and why documents are written, not whether. The sprint backlog, sprint goal and acceptance criteria are planning documents; regression tests are the test record; design is documented where it helps users, auditors or new members. Removing all documentation breaks traceability and handover.

quiz.q: Name the three Scrum roles and the three Scrum artifacts.
quiz.a: Roles: product owner, Scrum master, development team. Artifacts: product backlog, sprint backlog, increment.

quiz.q: Describe the TDD cycle and say why it makes refactoring safe.
quiz.a: Write a test for the next small behaviour and see it fail (red); write the least code that passes (green); refactor while tests stay green. The collected tests form a regression suite, so a structural change that breaks behaviour is caught at once.

quiz.q: Why do XP teams pair developers and rotate them across the code, rather than let one expert own a module?
quiz.a: Pairing is continuous review, so defects are caught while code is written, and knowledge spreads. Collective ownership and rotation remove the single point of failure, shorten fix time, and keep standards applied by many eyes.

quiz.q: Velocity is 10 points per sprint. Pair programming cuts capacity by 25%. Backlog: login 5, search 8, report 3, payment 13, help 2. How many sprints?
quiz.a: Total = 5+8+3+13+2 = 31. New velocity = 10 × 0.75 = 7.5. Sprints = ceil(31 ÷ 7.5) = ceil(4.13) = 5 sprints. Four sprints give 30 points, one point short.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry scales agile with frameworks such as SAFe and LeSS, and with Kanban boards that limit work in progress. Continuous integration and delivery pipelines are the industrial form of XP's continuous integration practice; see Unit 5. Modern variants add cycle time and lead time next to velocity.
